Approximate Muon with low-rank adapters

Ben Anson Affiliation: University of Bristol Affiliation: School of Mathematics Email: ben.lja@proton.me    Conor Houghton Affiliation: University of Bristol Affiliation: School of Engineering Mathematics and Technology Email: conor.houghton@bristol.ac.uk    Edward Milsom Affiliation: University of Bath Affiliation: Department of Computer Science Email: em846@bath.ac.uk
Abstract

The Muon optimizer shows clear benefits versus alternatives when pretraining neural networks. However, it is used less frequently for parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT). One potential reason is that the most common PEFT method, LoRA, does not naturally combine with Muon since it is not mathematically possible to orthogonalize the weight update given by a low-rank parameterization. In this paper, we address this issue by approximating the solution to a relaxed Muon objective in the low-rank setting via linearization and then least-squares. We provide an efficient implementation that uses matmul operations only, as opposed to more complex linear algebra decomposition routines. Our method, sMuon (small Muon), performs favourably across SFT and a ReLoRA pretraining experiment. While results are model- and eval-dependent, we find overall that using Muon for low-rank fine-tuning provides moderate performance improvements.

1 Introduction

Muon (22) is a neural network optimizer which orthogonalizes updates at each layer, equalizing all singular values. This can be interpreted as steepest descent under the spectral norm (3), thereby controlling the worst-case change to the layer as a linear operator, rather than viewing it as a flattened vector. Muon has demonstrated excellent results in the pretraining of LLMs, often outperforming AdamW, leading to its increasing adoption (26; 35; 24; 37; 40).

However, Muon is less commonly used for fine-tuning (FT), particularly PEFT (Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning, which reduces compute resource requirements). There are various reasons for this, including the fact that Muon FT has been shown to perform better with Muon-pretrained base models (26; 32), which are currently less common than AdamW-pretrained models. Perhaps the most glaring issue is that Muon does not straightforwardly combine with LoRA (19), the dominant PEFT method. In principle, Muon requires that we orthogonalize the descent step for the whole layer, but this is not generally realizable in the LoRA parameterization. Some approximation is therefore inevitable. The simplest and most common workaround is ‘per-factor Muon’, which ignores the geometry of the whole layer and orthogonalizes changes to BB and AA separately (32; 20; 23). Other works retain the whole layer’s geometry and introduce an approximation elsewhere, with 8 relaxing the Muon objective using the triangle inequality, and 7 recasting the problem as Riemannian optimization on a low-rank manifold.

However, we feel that alternative approaches that more closely fit with Muon’s original ‘steepest descent under the spectral norm’ motivation are still underexplored.

In this paper, we linearize the low-rank Muon objective to find the optimal descent step within the available parameter space. This solution effectively orthogonalizes the full layer’s gradient and projects it onto the appropriate low-rank subspace. Empirically, we find this retains a more uniform spectrum than alternatives such as per-factor Muon (Fig. 1) and LoRA-Muon (8). Furthermore, unlike Riemannion (7), our approach avoids expensive matrix decompositions. While our solution to the low-rank Muon problem is clean (Alg. 1), a naive implementation is computationally inefficient, as it requires orthogonalizing a large matrix. To address this, we introduce a mathematically equivalent formulation (Alg. 2) that is both fast and memory-efficient. By relying entirely on matrix multiplications, we are able to avoid the overhead from QR and SVD. Finally, we show that our optimizer, sMuon, achieves competitive performance across a range of commonsense and coding SFT benchmarks, as well as in ReLoRA pretraining experiments.

Our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We derive a method for training LoRA adapters with Muon by taking a first-order approximation of the spectral-norm-regularized steepest descent objective. The method is available in closed form, and requires less optimizer state than AdamW.

  • •

    We provide a matmul-only algorithm of the method, sMuon, that is efficient for modern hardware, with comparable speed to other Muon methods such as per-factor Muon and LoRA-Muon, while being significantly faster than Riemannion for larger LoRA rank.

  • •

    We run SFT experiments on four base models, three AdamW-pretrained and one Muon-pretrained, over eleven benchmarks to compare low-rank Muon optimizers. While results are model-dependent, we find that our optimizer gives strong performance, performing best on the Muon-pretrained model with the top accuracy in six out of eleven tasks with Moonlight-16B-A3B.

  • •

    In the ReLoRA pretraining setting, we illustrate that Muon LoRA methods are generally stronger than AdamW LoRA. Specifically we find that our method attains the lowest final validation loss, tying with Riemannion, but being ∼30%\sim\!30\% faster.

2 Related Work

Muon and spectral steepest descent

Muon orthogonalizes the gradient descent step for each weight matrix, so that the singular values of weight updates are equal (22). This update is exactly steepest descent under the spectral norm (4; 5). Muon has been shown to scale to billion- and trillion-parameter models for LLM pretraining, with considerable efficiency gains over AdamW (26; 24).

Muon for fine-tuning and optimizer mismatch

Although Muon excels at pretraining, it is used far less for fine-tuning. 26 note that fine-tuning an AdamW-pretrained model with Muon (or vice-versa) degrades performance. 32 suggest that the differing implicit biases of Adam and Muon are to blame, but that constraining the update (e.g. via LoRA) narrows the gap between Muon and AdamW fine-tuning. Muon’s increasing adoption makes this question more important than ever, and so in this paper we evaluate on both AdamW- and Muon-pretrained base models.

Geometry-aware and Muon-based LoRA optimizers

The most closely related works are 8 and 7; these both attempt to approximate a low-rank solution to the spectral-regularized gradient descent problem. LoRA-Muon (8) is derived by approximating the spectral steepest-descent optimization problem using the triangle inequality applied to the spectral norm regularizer, and then minimizing to first order. We similarly linearize (we expect second-order terms to be suitably small), but we avoid the triangle inequality, as this is not necessarily tight under the spectral norm. For their ‘Riemannion’ optimizer, 7 present the problem as Riemannian optimization on a constrained low-rank manifold. While some key ideas of this method are similar to our method (projecting onto the low-rank space), Riemannian optimization also involves a ‘retract’ step. One issue with their retraction is requiring a truncated SVD, which cannot be efficiently replaced with an efficient matmul-only approximation. In practice this leads to Riemannion being slower than alternatives, especially for larger LoRA rank. By contrast, we obtain the step using least squares on the orthogonalized gradient direction, avoiding expensive manifold constraints that don’t appear to benefit model performance. The PoLoRA (14) method is again similar to our work, but can be understood as a version of LoRA-Muon with additional preconditioning. LoRA-RITE (41) and Riemannian-preconditioned LoRA (43) attempt to keep the adapters invariant to parameterization. Another popular approach is to simply apply Muon to BB and AA independently (32; 20; 30). This ignores the geometry of the linear layer and causes the update to depend on the adapter parameterization, whereas our update is first-order parameterization-invariant (see App. A.3). Appendix C has a more detailed comparison of the various approaches.

Low-rank optimization beyond LoRA fine-tuning

Some works, such as Spectron (20), LORO (30), GaLore (45), and LoRA-Pre (39) target efficient low-rank pretraining, either through stabilization, or optimizer state compression. 17 accelerate Muon itself with a low-rank orthogonalization routine that exploits the low-rank structure of the gradient, but operate on full dense weight matrices rather than in the LoRA adapter setting. In contrast to all of these, our goal is a simple, principled, memory-efficient Muon update for the composite LoRA adapter Δ​W=B​A\Delta W=BA, rather than the full base weight W0W_{0}.

3 Background

3.1 Muon

Given a gradient matrix GW∈ℝd1×d2G_{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times d_{2}} for weight matrix W∈ℝd1×d2W\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times d_{2}}, Muon selects the step direction δ​W⋆∈ℝd1×d2\delta W^{\star}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times d_{2}} through a regularized minimization under the spectral norm ∥⋅∥2\|\cdot\|_{2} (largest singular value) (4):

δ​W⋆=arg​minδ​W⁡[⟨GW,δ​W⟩+λ2​‖δ​W‖22].\delta W^{\star}=\argmin_{\delta W}\;\left[\langle G_{W},\delta W\rangle+\frac{\lambda}{2}\|\delta W\|_{2}^{2}\right]. (1)

The solution, assuming GWG_{W} is full rank, is proportional to −msign⁡(GW)-\msign(G_{W}), where msign⁡(X)=U​V⊤\msign(X)=UV^{\top} for singular value decomposition X=U​Σ​V⊤X=U\Sigma V^{\top}, thereby orthogonalizing the gradient (or, in practice, the momentum). The solution is not unique for low-rank GWG_{W}, though we use the convention that msign⁡(X)=U​sign⁡(Σ)​V⊤\msign(X)=U\operatorname{sign}(\Sigma)V^{\top}, so that non-zero singular values are promoted, and the rest remain equal to zero.

3.2 LoRA

LoRA (19) is a parameter-efficient method for fine-tuning neural networks. LoRA adds adapters in the form Δ​W=B​A\Delta W=BA to the pretrained base weight W0W_{0} of a layer, with B∈ℝd1×rB\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times r} and A∈ℝr×d2A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{2}} where r≪d1,d2r\ll d_{1},d_{2}. Typically BB is initialized to zero to ensure that, initially, Δ​W=0\Delta W=0. The factors B,AB,A are usually chosen by minimizing the fine-tuning loss with the AdamW optimizer. We instead seek to find the analogue to Muon’s whitened update in the LoRA setting.

4 Method

Let Δ​W=B​A\Delta W=BA be the adapter with gradient GΔ​WG_{\Delta W}. Our goal is to find updates δ​B,δ​A\delta B,\delta A for the factors B,AB,A such that the implied update δ​Δ​W\delta\Delta W to the adapter Δ​W\Delta W has an approximately flat spectrum. We emphasize that simply orthogonalizing the factor updates δ​B,δ​A\delta B,\delta A does not imply that δ​Δ​W\delta\Delta W itself is orthogonal. Under spectral steepest descent, the optimal adapter update δ​Δ​W⋆\delta\Delta W^{\star} is given by

δ​Δ​W⋆=arg​minδ​Δ​W⁡[⟨GΔ​W,δ​Δ​W⟩+λ2​‖δ​Δ​W‖22].\delta\Delta W^{\star}=\argmin_{\delta\Delta W}\ \big[\,\big\langle G_{\Delta W},\,\delta\Delta W\big\rangle+\tfrac{\lambda}{2}\big\|\delta\Delta W\big\|_{2}^{2}\,\big]. (2)

If r=min⁡(d1,d2)r=\min(d_{1},\,d_{2}) then Δ​W\Delta W is full rank and this is an identical problem to Eq. (1), which is solved by whitening the gradient (4), i.e.,

δ​Δ​W⋆=−η​msign⁡(GΔ​W),\delta\Delta W^{\star}=-\eta\msign(G_{\Delta W}), (3)

where proportionality constants have been absorbed into η\eta. However, we do not get the same solution under a low-rank constraint r<min⁡(d1,d2)r<\min(d_{1},d_{2}). We have,

δ​Δ​W=(B+δ​B)​(A+δ​A)−B​A=δ​B​A+B​δ​A+δ​B​δ​A,\delta\Delta W=(B+\delta B)(A+\delta A)-BA=\delta B\,A+B\,\delta A+\delta B\,\delta A, (4)

but generally it is not possible to find δ​B,δ​A\delta B,\,\delta A that satisfy δ​Δ​W=−η​msign⁡(GΔ​W)\delta\Delta W=-\eta\msign(G_{\Delta W}). The problem here is that the change δ​Δ​W\delta\Delta W has rank at most 2​r2r, but msign⁡(GΔ​W)\msign(G_{\Delta W}) is usually full rank.

We proceed by writing Eq. (2) in terms of the adapter matrices,

(δ​B⋆,δ​A⋆)=arg​minδ​B,δ​A⁡[⟨GΔ​W,δ​B​A+B​δ​A+δ​B​δ​A⟩+λ2​‖δ​B​A+B​δ​A+δ​B​δ​A‖22].(\delta B^{\star},\delta A^{\star})=\argmin_{\delta B,\delta A}\ \bigg[\big\langle G_{\Delta W},\,\delta B\,A+B\,\delta A+\delta B\,\delta A\big\rangle+\tfrac{\lambda}{2}\big\|\delta B\,A+B\,\delta A+\delta B\,\delta A\big\|_{2}^{2}\bigg]. (5)

This is a non-linear optimization problem due to the second-order terms, and it has no known closed-form solution. For small updates δ​B,δ​A\delta B,\delta A, we approximate by dropping these second-order terms, giving

(δ​B⋆,δ​A⋆)=arg​minδ​B,δ​A⁡[⟨GΔ​W,δ​B​A+B​δ​A⟩+λ2​‖δ​B​A+B​δ​A‖22].(\delta B^{\star},\delta A^{\star})=\argmin_{\delta B,\delta A}\ \bigg[\big\langle G_{\Delta W},\,\delta B\,A+B\,\delta A\big\rangle+\tfrac{\lambda}{2}\big\|\delta B\,A+B\,\delta A\big\|_{2}^{2}\bigg]. (6)

Since it is generally not possible to achieve the rank-unconstrained minimum, we instead try to get as close as possible. We solve a least-squares problem for the linearized update map (overloading the notation δ​B⋆,δ​A⋆\delta B^{\star},\,\delta A^{\star} for convenience),

(δ​B⋆,δ​A⋆)=arg​minδ​B,δ​A⁡‖δ​Δ​W⋆−(δ​B​A+B​δ​A)‖F2.(\delta B^{\star},\delta A^{\star})=\argmin_{\delta B,\,\delta A}\ \big\|\,\delta\Delta W^{\star}-(\delta B\,A+B\,\delta A)\,\big\|_{F}^{2}. (7)

Taking gradients of the objective w.r.t. δ​B\delta B and δ​A\delta A and setting to zero, we have,

0\displaystyle 0 =−2​(δ​Δ​W⋆−δ​B​A−B​δ​A)​A⊤,\displaystyle=-2(\delta\Delta W^{\star}-\delta B\,A-B\,\delta A)A^{\top}, (8a)
0\displaystyle 0 =−2​B⊤​(δ​Δ​W⋆−δ​B​A−B​δ​A).\displaystyle=-2B^{\top}(\delta\Delta W^{\star}-\delta B\,A-B\,\delta A). (8b)

Assuming BB and AA have full rank, right-multiplying Eq. (8a) by (A​A⊤)−1(AA^{\top})^{-1} and left-multiplying Eq. (8b) by (B⊤​B)−1(B^{\top}B)^{-1} gives

δ​Δ​W⋆​A†\displaystyle\delta\Delta W^{\star}A^{\dagger} =δ​B​A​A†+B​δ​A​A†\displaystyle=\delta B\,AA^{\dagger}+B\,\delta A\,A^{\dagger} =δ​B+B​δ​A​A†,\displaystyle=\delta B+B\delta A\,A^{\dagger}, (9a)
B†​δ​Δ​W⋆\displaystyle B^{\dagger}\delta\Delta W^{\star} =B†​δ​B​A+B†​B​δ​A\displaystyle=B^{\dagger}\delta B\,A+B^{\dagger}B\,\delta A =B†​δ​B​A+δ​A,\displaystyle=B^{\dagger}\delta B\,A+\delta A, (9b)

where B†=(B⊤​B)−1​B⊤B^{\dagger}=(B^{\top}B)^{-1}B^{\top} and A†=A⊤​(A​A⊤)−1A^{\dagger}=A^{\top}(AA^{\top})^{-1} are the Moore-Penrose inverses satisfying B†​B=I=A​A†B^{\dagger}B=I=AA^{\dagger}. Note that the minimizer is not unique: if (δ​B,δ​A)(\delta B,\delta A) is a minimizer of Eq. (7), then so is (δ​B+B​S,δ​A−S​A)(\delta B+BS,\delta A-SA) since,

δ​B​A+B​δ​A=(δ​B+B​S)​A+B⁡(δ​A−S​A).\displaystyle\delta B\,A+B\,\delta A=(\delta B+BS)A+B\,(\delta A-SA). (10)

Rearranging Eq. (9b), and setting S=−B†​δ​BS=-B^{\dagger}\delta B means that

δ​A⋆\displaystyle\delta A^{\star} =B†​δ​Δ​W⋆\displaystyle=B^{\dagger}\delta\Delta W^{\star} (11a)
is one particular minimizer, and then substituting into Eq. (9a) gives the corresponding δ​B⋆\delta B^{\star},
δ​B⋆\displaystyle\delta B^{\star} =(I−B​B†)​δ​Δ​W⋆​A†.\displaystyle=(I-BB^{\dagger})\delta\Delta W^{\star}A^{\dagger}. (11b)

4.1 Low-rank gradients

While the solution (δ​B⋆,δ​A⋆)(\delta B^{\star},\,\delta A^{\star}) given by Eq. (11) is simple, it is not efficiently computed. The δ​Δ​W⋆=−η​msign⁡(GΔ​W)\delta\Delta W^{\star}=-\eta\msign(G_{\Delta W}) term requires orthogonalization of a large matrix (remember that GΔ​W∈ℝd1×d2G_{\Delta W}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times d_{2}}), which we would like to avoid. Fortunately, we do not actually require the full gradient GΔ​WG_{\Delta W}, and can instead use the low-rank gradient,

H:=GΔ​W−(I−PB)​GΔ​W​(I−PA)=PB​GΔ​W+(I−PB)​GΔ​W​PA,H:=G_{\Delta W}-(I-P_{B})\,G_{\Delta W}\,(I-P_{A})=P_{B}G_{\Delta W}+(I-P_{B})G_{\Delta W}P_{A}, (12)

where PB=B​B†P_{B}=BB^{\dagger} and PA=A†​AP_{A}=A^{\dagger}A are projections onto the column space of BB and row space of AA respectively. The low-rank gradient HH is the projection of the gradient onto the subspace of weight updates that the current LoRA adapter can express. The two gradients HH and GΔ​WG_{\Delta W} are first-order equivalent, in the sense that for any δ​B,δ​A\delta B,\delta A,

⟨GΔ​W,δ​B​A+B​δ​A⟩=⟨H,δ​B​A+B​δ​A⟩.\langle G_{\Delta W},\,\delta B\,A+B\delta A\rangle=\langle H,\delta B\,A+B\delta A\rangle. (13)

Thus when linearizing the Muon objective, we can replace GΔ​WG_{\Delta W} with HH to obtain,

(δ​B,δ​A)=arg​minδ​B,δ​A⁡[⟨H,δ​B​A+B​δ​A⟩+λ2​‖δ​B​A+B​δ​A‖22].\displaystyle(\delta B,\delta A)=\argmin_{\delta B,\delta A}\left[\langle H,\,\delta B\,A+B\,\delta A\rangle+\tfrac{\lambda}{2}\|\delta B\,A+B\,\delta A\|_{2}^{2}\right]. (14)

In particular, this means we use δ​Δ​W⋆=−η​msign⁡(H)\delta\Delta W^{\star}=-\eta\msign(H). We show in the next section how this can be exploited to compute the update efficiently.

4.2 Efficient, matmul-only computation

We now show how to compute the descent steps δ​B⋆\delta B^{\star} and δ​A⋆\delta A^{\star} efficiently. One of the principal advantages of our method versus Riemannion is that it permits a matmul-only solution — Riemannion requires truncated SVDs during the retraction step, which makes parallelization/batching of computation slower (see Table 4). In particular, the most expensive operations required are d×rd\times r matmuls, which are easily optimized with deep learning libraries.

The gradients for BB and AA are GB=GΔ​W​A⊤G_{B}=G_{\Delta W}A^{\top} and GA=B⊤​GΔ​WG_{A}=B^{\top}G_{\Delta W} respectively; the low-rank gradient of Eq. (12) can therefore be written as,

H=B(B⊤​B)−1​GA⏟=:X+(I−PB)​GB​(A​A⊤)−1⏟=:YA,H=B\underbrace{(B^{\top}B)^{-1}G_{A}}_{=:\,X}\;+\;\underbrace{(I-P_{B})\,G_{B}\,(AA^{\top})^{-1}}_{=:\,Y}\,A, (15)

where X∈ℝr×d2X\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{2}} and Y∈ℝd1×rY\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times r}. Assuming B,A,X,YB,\,A,\,X,\,Y have rank rr, we have rank⁡(H)≤2​r\operatorname{rank}(H)\leq 2r.

msign⁡(H)=U​msign⁡(U⊤​H​V)​V⊤.\msign(H)=U\,\msign(U^{\top}HV)\,V^{\top}. (16)

where we used B†​U1=SBB^{\dagger}U_{1}=S_{B} and B†​U2=0B^{\dagger}U_{2}=0. Similarly,
δ​B⋆=−η⁡(I−PB)​U​Ω​V⊤​A†=−η​U2​Ω21​SA,\displaystyle\delta B^{\star}=-\eta(I-P_{B})U\Omega V^{\top}A^{\dagger}=-\eta U_{2}\,\Omega_{21}\,S_{A}, (21b)

using (I−PB)​U1=0(I-P_{B})U_{1}=0, (I−PB)​U2=U2(I-P_{B})U_{2}=U_{2}, V1⊤​A†=SAV_{1}^{\top}A^{\dagger}=S_{A}, and V2⊤​A†=0V_{2}^{\top}A^{\dagger}=0.

All components of δ​B⋆\delta B^{\star} and δ​A⋆\delta A^{\star} can be computed with matmuls, matrix inverse roots, and msign\msign. In practice, both the r×rr\times r inverse square roots and the msign\msign’s can be evaluated with matrix polynomial iterations (1; 44), which are themselves sequences of matrix products.

4.3 Algorithm

We combine the above updates with split weight decay (8) to match the weight decay dynamics of full-parameter training to first order, and momentum projection (inspired by momentum transport of 7, see App. A.3 for details) to ensure reparameterization invariance, yielding the sMuon optimizer for LoRA adapters. We provide Alg. 1 as a pedagogical version, while Alg. 2 incorporates the efficient matmul-only computations from the previous section.

We also discuss a more numerically stable variant in Appendix B. One cause for concern is the practice of initializing the adapter Δ​W=B​A=0\Delta W=BA=0, and then computing inverse roots of B⊤​BB^{\top}B and A​A⊤AA^{\top}. We found that, despite initializing Δ​W=0\Delta W=0, calculating inverse roots of A​A⊤AA^{\top} and B⊤​BB^{\top}B was not an issue when using jitter and a semi-orthonormal BB, A=0A=0 initialization.

5 Experiments

We compare sMuon to regular LoRA with AdamW, per-factor Muon (LoRA with Muon applied to each adapter weight BB and AA individually), LoRA-Muon (8), and Riemannion (7). We evaluated on standard commonsense (12; 11; 42; 29; 6; 34) and coding (10; 2) benchmarks after training with SFT. We experimented with four models, Llama-3.2-3B (16), Qwen2.5-3B (33), DeepSeek-V2-Lite (13), and Moonlight-16B-A3B (26). The first two models are dense models; the last two are sparse MoE models. The Moonlight model is of particular note because it was pretrained with Muon, whereas the others are all AdamW-pretrained. We also tested the methods in a pretraining setting using ReLoRA (25) which periodically merges and refreshes the adapter. We tuned the learning rate for each method and model, with example learning rate sweeps for the commonsense tasks shown in Appendix E.

While our results are both model- and eval-dependent, sMuon performs strongly overall, especially when combined with the Moonlight-16B-A3B base model, a Muon-pretrained model (Tables 1 and 2). sMuon also achieved the joint-best validation loss in the ReLoRA pretraining setting (Table 3). We attribute performance gains, particularly over AdamW and per-factor Muon, to more accurately approximating the Muon objective.

Experiment details

LoRA-Muon and Riemannion were chosen as baselines in addition to the simpler AdamW and per-factor Muon baselines as these are the most similar to our method. Unfortunately, we could not find implementations for LoRA-Muon or Riemannion, so we implemented these ourselves. For Riemannion and our method, we use an A=0A=0 and BB orthonormal initialization, and for the remaining methods we used a standard initialization (B=0B=0, AA random Gaussian). We scale the learning rate to approximately match AdamW RMS for all Muon optimizers (for details see App. A.1). For all experiments, we used weight decay 0.010.01, momentum 0.90.9, inserted LoRA adapters into all hidden layers (except the router for models with MoE). We used GH200 for all experiments except to produce Table 4 for which we used A100. We used bf16 to store weights and optimizer states, but used fp32 to compute the step for Riemannion, sMuon, and LoRA-Muon.

For the ReLoRA experiments (25), we started with the modded-nanogpt codebase at ‘record 8’ (21), which trains a 162M parameter transformer from scratch (using features including QK-norm, ReLU2 activations) on the FineWeb dataset (31), and evaluates on a 10M token validation set. We initialize LoRA adapters with rank 64, and train for a total of 3000 steps; every 500 steps we merge the adapters into the base weights and reinitialize the adapters; we use a cosine decay learning rate schedule, though after each merge+reinitialization, we also reset the learning rate to zero and warm back up to the target learning rate over 50 steps (this is also known as a jagged cosine schedule). We swept learning rates in 3e-4, 6e-4, 1e-3, 3e-3, 6e-3, 1e-2.

For the HumanEval (10) and MBPP (2) coding evals, we fine-tuned for 3 epochs on completing Python functions from the CodeAlpaca dataset (9). For the MMLU (18) eval, we fine-tuned on a 50/50 mixture of FLAN (27) and MMLU training subset. For the remaining evals, we trained on a mixture of FLAN and CommonsenseQA (36), and training subset for each eval. All SFT evals were 0-shot. For SFT training runs, we used α=32\alpha=32, r=16r=16, gradient clipping (clipping at 11), and we used roughly 2162^{16} tokens per batch.

Muon-based LoRA is strongest on the Muon-pretrained model

We originally hypothesized that Muon-based LoRA methods might perform better with Moonlight, since it is a Muon-pretrained model. We do find some evidence for this when aggregating over all benchmarks in Tables 1 and 2: AdamW only achieves top performance on one of the eleven tasks, while sMuon is best for six. Some methods are markedly below others on certain tasks (e.g. per-factor Muon with Llama-3.2-3B on HumanEval, Table 2). This could be due to optimizer instabilities or noise in the benchmarks or selection procedure.

Benefits of Muon pretraining remain with ReLoRA

The ReLoRA experiment (Table 3) removes optimizer mismatch entirely by training from scratch. The separation between optimizer families is clear. Every Muon-based method achieves lower validation loss than LoRA+AdamW. One explanation for the strong Muon performance is amplification of the small but real signal in the long tail of the gradient’s spectrum (38).

Efficiency gain from the matmul-only implementation

Table 4 compares step times for the different optimizers. AdamW is the fastest; the only computation required by AdamW is element-wise, meaning that data communication is likely to be the largest overhead. Per-factor Muon is the next fastest, because computation is dominated by two msign⁡(⋅)\msign(\cdot) computations (that can be batched). Both LoRA-Muon and sMuon require more matmuls than per-factor Muon, but the compute time is still negligible compared to the forward+backward pass time per step of ∼1.4\sim 1.4s. On the other hand, computing the Riemannion step is much slower, adding ∼50%\sim 50\% overhead to the forward+backward pass when r=64r=64, and even longer for r=128r=128. The computation is slow because Riemannion requires thin QRs and 2​r×2​r2r\times 2r SVDs, which add overhead for larger rr. Note that the retraction step in Riemannion specifically requires truncated SVD, which cannot be replaced by a more efficient Newton-Schulz algorithm. We found that compiling the core computation (i.e. the matmuls), and batching the computation leads to big efficiency gains with all the Muon methods except Riemannion.

6 Conclusion

We considered optimizing low-rank adapters using an approximate form of Muon. The resulting step is available in closed form, is invariant to the adapter parameterization (B,A)↦(B​S,S−1​A)(B,A)\mapsto(BS,S^{-1}A) and is cheap, costing O⁡(r2​(d1+d2)+r3)O(r^{2}(d_{1}+d_{2})+r^{3}) time and O⁡(r​max⁡(d1,d2))O(r\max(d_{1},d_{2})) memory, using less optimizer state than LoRA+AdamW. Our implementation, sMuon, has empirically flatter spectra than per-factor Muon and out-performs other methods on the Moonlight Muon-pretrained model. In ReLoRA pretraining every Muon-based method beats AdamW, with sMuon and Riemannion the strongest. In general, by respecting the geometry of the full layer, rather than treating BB and AA as unrelated matrices, we often benefit, and there is little extra cost.

Appendix A Other algorithmic details

We discuss some pre-existing techniques that we incorporated into sMuon.

A.1 Match AdamW RMS

Inspired by 26, we adopt a learning rate adjustment. The full-parameter scaling is 0.2​max⁡(din,dout)0.2\sqrt{\max(d_{\text{in}},d_{\text{out}})}, with the overall update, including weight decay, becoming

x←x−λ​η​x−0.2​η​max⁡(din,dout)⋅δ​x.\displaystyle x\leftarrow x-\lambda\eta x-0.2\eta\sqrt{\max(d_{\text{in}},d_{\text{out}})}\,\cdot\,\delta x. (22)

To match this in the LoRA setting, we used

x←x−λ​η​x−0.2​η​din​dout/r⋅δ​x.\displaystyle x\leftarrow x-\lambda\eta x-0.2\eta\sqrt{d_{\text{in}}d_{\text{out}}/r}\,\cdot\,\delta x. (23)

We loosely justify this heuristic: assume the weight update δ​Δ​W\delta\Delta W is orthogonalized. The rank of δ​Δ​W\delta\Delta W is at most 2​r2r (it can be written as the difference of two rank rr matrices), and therefore ‖δ​Δ​W‖F2≤2​r\|\delta\Delta W\|_{F}^{2}\leq 2r. So ‖δ​Δ​W‖rms≤2​r/(din​dout)\|\delta\Delta W\|_{\text{rms}}\leq\sqrt{2r/(d_{\text{in}}d_{\text{out}})}. We absorb the 2\sqrt{2} factor, and use a scale of 0.2​din​dout/r0.2\sqrt{d_{\text{in}}d_{\text{out}}/r}.

A.2 Split weight decay

If we apply weight decay to BB and AA separately, this gives different dynamics compared to full-parameter training. Concretely,

At+1\displaystyle A_{t+1} =(1−η​λ)​At−η​δ​A,Bt+1=(1−η​λ)​Bt−η​δ​B\displaystyle=(1-\eta\lambda)A_{t}-\eta\,\delta A,\quad B_{t+1}=(1-\eta\lambda)B_{t}-\eta\,\delta B
⟹δ​Δ​W\displaystyle\implies\delta\Delta W =[(1−η​λ)​Bt−η​δ​B]​[(1−η​λ)​At−η​δ​A]−Bt​At\displaystyle=\big[(1-\eta\lambda)B_{t}-\eta\,\delta B\big]\big[(1-\eta\lambda)A_{t}-\eta\,\delta A\big]-B_{t}A_{t}
=−[1−(1−η​λ)2]​Bt​At−η⁡(1−η​λ)​(Bt​δ​A+δ​B​At)+O⁡(η2),\displaystyle=-\big[1-(1-\eta\lambda)^{2}\big]B_{t}A_{t}-\eta(1-\eta\lambda)\big(B_{t}\,\delta A+\delta B\,A_{t}\big)+O(\eta^{2}),

which is not recognizable in terms of full-parameter dynamics. We adopt the split weight decay of 8 to preserve the first-order weight decay dynamics. Setting s=1−λ​ηs=\sqrt{1-\lambda\eta}, LoRA factors update as,

At+1\displaystyle A_{t+1} =s​At−ηs​δ​A,\displaystyle=s\,A_{t}-\tfrac{\eta}{s}\,\delta A, (24)
Bt+1\displaystyle B_{t+1} =s​Bt−ηs​δ​B.\displaystyle=s\,B_{t}-\tfrac{\eta}{s}\,\delta B. (25)

Expanding the resulting weight change δ​Δ​W=Bt+1​At+1−Bt​At\delta\Delta W=B_{t+1}A_{t+1}-B_{t}A_{t} gives,

δ​Δ​W\displaystyle\delta\Delta W =(s​Bt−ηs​δ​B)​(s​At−ηs​δ​A)−Bt​At\displaystyle=\left(sB_{t}-\tfrac{\eta}{s}\,\delta B\right)\left(sA_{t}-\tfrac{\eta}{s}\,\delta A\right)-B_{t}A_{t} (26)
=s2​Bt​At−η⁡(δ​B​At+Bt​δ​A)+η2s2​δ​B​δ​A−Bt​At\displaystyle=s^{2}B_{t}A_{t}-\eta(\delta B\,A_{t}+B_{t}\,\delta A)+\tfrac{\eta^{2}}{s^{2}}\,\delta B\,\delta A-B_{t}A_{t} (27)
=(s2−1)​Bt​At−η⁡(δ​B​At+Bt​δ​A)+η2s2​δ​B​δ​A\displaystyle=(s^{2}-1)B_{t}A_{t}-\eta(\delta B\,A_{t}+B_{t}\,\delta A)+\tfrac{\eta^{2}}{s^{2}}\,\delta B\,\delta A (28)
=−λ​η​Δ​Wt⏟decay term−η⁡(δ​B​At+Bt​δ​A)⏟gradient term+O⁡(η2)\displaystyle=\underbrace{-\lambda\eta\,\Delta W_{t}}_{\text{decay term}}-\underbrace{\eta(\delta B\,A_{t}+B_{t}\,\delta A)}_{\text{gradient term}}+O(\eta^{2}) (29)

which we identify as having the dynamics of decoupled weight decay [28].

A.3 Invariance to parameterization

In practice, we orthogonalize a momentum rather than a raw gradient. The natural choice for momentum accumulation is MA←β​MA+(1−β)​GAM_{A}\leftarrow\beta M_{A}+(1-\beta)G_{A} and MB←β​MB+(1−β)​GBM_{B}\leftarrow\beta M_{B}+(1-\beta)G_{B}, and to reconstruct the effective momentum by substituting them for GA,GBG_{A},\,G_{B} in the equation factorizing HH,

H¯t=(Bt†)⊤​MA,t+(I−PBt)​MB,t​(At†)⊤.\bar{H}_{t}=(B_{t}^{\dagger})^{\top}M_{A,t}+(I-P_{B_{t}})\,M_{B,t}(A_{t}^{\dagger})^{\top}. (30)

Here, GB=GΔ​W​A⊤G_{B}=G_{\Delta W}A^{\top} and GA=B⊤​GΔ​WG_{A}=B^{\top}G_{\Delta W} are the gradients of the adapter matrices BB and AA respectively. Consider two training runs, (Bt,At)(B_{t},\,A_{t}) and (Bt′,At′)(B_{t}^{\prime},A_{t}^{\prime}), that differ only in their parameterizations at each step,

(Bt′,At′)=(Bt​St,St−1​At).(B_{t}^{\prime},A_{t}^{\prime})=(B_{t}S_{t},\;S_{t}^{-1}A_{t}). (31)

Since Δ​Wt′=Bt′​At′=Bt​At=Δ​Wt\Delta W_{t}^{\prime}=B_{t}^{\prime}A_{t}^{\prime}=B_{t}A_{t}=\Delta W_{t}, we want the optimizer to take equivalent steps throughout training, regardless of StS_{t}. For this, it is necessary that H¯t′=H¯t\bar{H}_{t}^{\prime}=\bar{H}_{t}.

Without transporting momentum buffers

The adapter gradients in the primed run are GA,k′=(Bk′)⊤​GΔ​W,k=Sk⊤​GA,kG_{A,k}^{\prime}=(B_{k}^{\prime})^{\top}G_{\Delta W,k}=S_{k}^{\top}G_{A,k} and GB,k′=GΔ​W,k​(Ak′)⊤=GB,k​Sk−⁣⊤G_{B,k}^{\prime}=G_{\Delta W,k}(A_{k}^{\prime})^{\top}=G_{B,k}S_{k}^{-\top}. Unrolling the EMA, we have,

MA,t′=∑k≤t(1−β)​βt−k​Sk⊤​GA,k,MB,t′=∑k≤t(1−β)​βt−k​GB,k​Sk−⁣⊤.M_{A,t}^{\prime}=\sum_{k\leq t}(1-\beta)\beta^{t-k}\,S_{k}^{\top}G_{A,k},\qquad M_{B,t}^{\prime}=\sum_{k\leq t}(1-\beta)\beta^{t-k}\,G_{B,k}S_{k}^{-\top}. (32)

Thus, the ‘primed’ run’s effective momentum is,

H¯t′=∑k≤t(1−β)​βt−k​[(Bt†)⊤​St−⁣⊤​Sk⊤​GA,k+(I−PBt)​GB,k​Sk−⁣⊤​St⊤​(At†)⊤],\bar{H}_{t}^{\prime}=\sum_{k\leq t}(1-\beta)\beta^{t-k}\Big[(B_{t}^{\dagger})^{\top}\,S_{t}^{-\top}S_{k}^{\top}\,G_{A,k}\;+\;(I-P_{B_{t}})\,G_{B,k}\,S_{k}^{-\top}S_{t}^{\top}\,(A_{t}^{\dagger})^{\top}\Big], (33)

which differs from H¯t\bar{H}_{t} by the factors St−⁣⊤​Sk⊤S_{t}^{-\top}S_{k}^{\top} and Sk−⁣⊤​St⊤S_{k}^{-\top}S_{t}^{\top}. These are the identity only when Sk=StS_{k}=S_{t}, so in general H¯t′≠H¯t\bar{H}_{t}^{\prime}\neq\bar{H}_{t}.

With momentum transport

We fix the issue by re-deriving the buffers from H¯\bar{H} against the factors as they stand at the end of the step,

MA←B⊤​H¯,MB←H¯​A⊤.M_{A}\leftarrow B^{\top}\bar{H},\qquad M_{B}\leftarrow\bar{H}A^{\top}. (34)

Geometrically, this projects H¯\bar{H} onto the space in which our updates, δ​B​A+B​δ​A\delta B\,A+B\,\delta A, exist. The momenta at the next step are then,

MA,t+1\displaystyle M_{A,t+1} =Bt+1⊤​(β​H¯t+(1−β)​GΔ​W,t+1),\displaystyle=B_{t+1}^{\top}\big(\beta\bar{H}_{t}+(1-\beta)G_{\Delta W,t+1}\big), (35)
MB,t+1\displaystyle M_{B,t+1} =(β​H¯t+(1−β)​GΔ​W,t+1)​At+1⊤.\displaystyle=\big(\beta\bar{H}_{t}+(1-\beta)G_{\Delta W,t+1}\big)A_{t+1}^{\top}. (36)

Assuming H¯t′=H¯t\bar{H}_{t}^{\prime}=\bar{H}_{t}, we have MA,t+1′=(Bt+1′)⊤​(β​H¯t+(1−β)​GΔ​W,t+1)=St+1⊤​MA,t+1M_{A,t+1}^{\prime}=(B_{t+1}^{\prime})^{\top}\big(\beta\bar{H}_{t}+(1-\beta)G_{\Delta W,t+1}\big)=S_{t+1}^{\top}M_{A,t+1} and similarly MB,t+1′=MB,t+1​St+1−⁣⊤M_{B,t+1}^{\prime}=M_{B,t+1}S_{t+1}^{-\top}. By further substitution,

H¯t+1′\displaystyle\bar{H}_{t+1}^{\prime} =(St+1−1​Bt+1†)⊤​St+1⊤​MA,t+1+(I−PBt+1)​MB,t+1​St+1−⁣⊤​(At+1†​St+1)⊤\displaystyle=\big(S_{t+1}^{-1}B_{t+1}^{\dagger}\big)^{\top}S_{t+1}^{\top}M_{A,t+1}+(I-P_{B_{t+1}})\,M_{B,t+1}S_{t+1}^{-\top}\big(A_{t+1}^{\dagger}S_{t+1}\big)^{\top}
=(Bt+1†)⊤​St+1−⁣⊤​St+1⊤⏟I​MA,t+1+(I−PBt+1)​MB,t+1​St+1−⁣⊤​St+1⊤⏟I​(At+1†)⊤\displaystyle=(B_{t+1}^{\dagger})^{\top}\underbrace{S_{t+1}^{-\top}S_{t+1}^{\top}}_{I}M_{A,t+1}+(I-P_{B_{t+1}})\,M_{B,t+1}\underbrace{S_{t+1}^{-\top}S_{t+1}^{\top}}_{I}(A_{t+1}^{\dagger})^{\top}
=H¯t+1.\displaystyle=\;\bar{H}_{t+1}.

So long as we project H¯\bar{H} into the momentum buffers at every step, the two runs will orthogonalize the same matrix, and therefore the realized steps will agree.

Appendix B Alternative stable algorithm

See Alg. 3, a mathematically equivalent but more stable alternative to Alg. 2 from the main text. In particular, we perform two orthogonalization steps [15] to help preserve orthogonality to machine precision, and include relative jitter to help stability for larger rr. Another difference between Alg. 2 and 3 is that we use slightly different U2U_{2}, V2.V_{2}. Alg. 3 uses U2=msign⁡(Y~)U_{2}=\msign(\tilde{Y}), where Y=Y~​SA2Y=\tilde{Y}S_{A}^{2}, and V2=msign⁡(Z~)V_{2}=\msign(\tilde{Z}), where Z=Z~​SB2Z=\tilde{Z}S_{B}^{2}. This is possible because the property we need is col⁡(Y)=col⁡(Y~)\operatorname{col}(Y)=\operatorname{col}(\tilde{Y}), and similar for ZZ/Z~\tilde{Z}, which is true when SBS_{B} and SAS_{A} are invertible (we assume this to be the case).

One can also consider additional interventions, such as replacing msign(X)=X(X⊤X)−1/2\msign(X)=X(X^{\top}X)^{-1/2} for X∈ℝd×rX\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r} with X​𝚒𝚗𝚟𝚛𝚘𝚘𝚝​(X⊤​X)X\,\mathtt{invroot}(X^{\top}X). The latter is slightly faster for small rr (since X⊤​X∈ℝr×rX^{\top}X\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r}), but we found the benefits to be small in practice.

Appendix C Comparison of Muon-based LoRA optimizers

Every method that combines Muon with LoRA has the same obstruction: Muon requires a step along msign⁡(GΔ​W)\msign(G_{\Delta W}), but a gradient step for a LoRA adapter is constrained inside the set 𝒯={Z:(I−PB)​Z​(I−PA)=0}\mathcal{T}=\{Z:(I-P_{B})Z(I-P_{A})=0\}. The ideal step msign⁡(GΔ​W)\msign(G_{\Delta W}) is not in general within this set, thus different methods make different approximations. We compare the different methods in Table 5.

Appendix D Optimality of the sMuon step

We show in Lemma 1 that our particular choice of δ​A\delta A and δ​B\delta B (a) is, to first order, as close as possible to the target step −η​msign⁡(H)-\eta\msign(H), and (b) while the minimum is not unique in terms of steps (δ​B,δ​A)(\delta B,\,\delta A), it is unique in terms of the first-order change to the whole linear layer.

Lemma 1.

Let B∈ℝd1×rB\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times r} have full column rank and A∈ℝr×d2A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{2}} have full row rank. Let PB=B​B†P_{B}=BB^{\dagger} and PA=A†​AP_{A}=A^{\dagger}A, let GΔ​WG_{\Delta W} be the adapter gradient, and let H=GΔ​W−(I−PB)​GΔ​W​(I−PA)H=G_{\Delta W}-(I-P_{B})\,G_{\Delta W}\,(I-P_{A}). Write δ​Δ​W=(B+δ​B)​(A+δ​A)−B​A\delta\Delta W=(B+\delta B)(A+\delta A)-BA and δ​Δ​W⋆=−η​msign⁡(H)\delta\Delta W^{\star}=-\eta\,\msign(H). Consider updates of the form δ​B=O⁡(η)\delta B=O(\eta), δ​A=O⁡(η)\delta A=O(\eta), then

‖δ​Δ​W⋆−δ​Δ​W‖F=‖η​msign⁡(H)+δ​B​A+B​δ​A‖F+O⁡(η2),\|\delta\Delta W^{\star}-\delta\Delta W\|_{F}\;=\;\,\|\eta\msign(H)+\delta B\,A+B\delta A\|_{F}\;+\;O(\eta^{2}), (37)
  1. 1.

    The choice δ​A=−η​B†​msign⁡(H)\delta A=-\eta\,B^{\dagger}\,\msign(H), δ​B=−η⁡(I−PB)​msign⁡(H)​A†\delta B=-\eta\,(I-P_{B})\,\msign(H)\,A^{\dagger} minimizes ‖δ​Δ​W⋆−δ​Δ​W‖F\|\delta\Delta W^{\star}-\delta\Delta W\|_{F} to first order.

  2. 2.

    The first-order minimizer is not unique. If (δ​B,δ​A)(\delta B,\,\delta A) is a minimizing pair, then so is (δ​B−B​S,δ​A+S​A)(\delta B-BS,\ \delta A+SA) with S∈ℝr×rS\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r}, provided that S=O⁡(η)S=O(\eta). Every first-order minimizer realizes the same overall update,

    δ​Δ​W=−η⁡[PB​msign⁡(H)+(I−PB)​msign⁡(H)​PA]+O⁡(η2).\delta\Delta W\;=\;-\eta\big[P_{B}\msign(H)+(I-P_{B})\msign(H)P_{A}\big]+O(\eta^{2}). (38)
Proof.

Since B†​B=I=A​A†∈ℝr×rB^{\dagger}B=I=AA^{\dagger}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r}, we have (I−PB)​B=0(I-P_{B})B=0 and A⁡(I−PA)=0A(I-P_{A})=0. Write M=msign⁡(H)M=\msign(H), δ​B=η​b\delta B=\eta b, δ​A=η​a\delta A=\eta a with a,ba,b bounded independently of η\eta. Then

δ​Δ​W⋆−δ​Δ​W=−η⁡(M+b​A+B​a)+O⁡(η2)\delta\Delta W^{\star}-\delta\Delta W\;=\;-\eta\,(M+bA+Ba)+O(\eta^{2})

and the reverse triangle inequality gives Eq. (37). It therefore suffices to minimize the leading coefficient ‖M+b​A+B​a‖F\|M+bA+Ba\|_{F}.

Any X∈ℝd1×d2X\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times d_{2}} admits the decomposition

X=PB​X​PA+PB​X​(I−PA)+(I−PB)​X​PA+(I−PB)​X​(I−PA),X=P_{B}XP_{A}+P_{B}X(I-P_{A})+(I-P_{B})XP_{A}+(I-P_{B})X(I-P_{A}),

a sum of four mutually Frobenius-orthogonal terms. We have (I−PB)​(b​A+B​a)​(I−PA)=0(I-P_{B})(bA+Ba)(I-P_{A})=0, so

‖M+b​A+B​a‖F2≥‖(I−PB)​M​(I−PA)‖F2.\|M+bA+Ba\|_{F}^{2}\;\geq\;\|(I-P_{B})\,M\,(I-P_{A})\|_{F}^{2}.

Crucially, the RHS is independent of the choice of b,ab,\,a. We get equality when the other three blocks of the decomposition are zero, which they are for M+b​A+B​aM+bA+Ba,

PB\displaystyle P_{B} (M+b​A+B​a)​PA+PB​(M+b​A+B​a)​(I−PA)+(I−PB)​(M+b​A+B​a)​PA\displaystyle(M+bA+Ba)P_{A}+P_{B}(M+bA+Ba)(I-P_{A})+(I-P_{B})(M+bA+Ba)P_{A}
=PB​(M+b​A+B​a)+(I−PB)​(M+b​A+B​a)​PA\displaystyle=P_{B}(M+bA+Ba)\;+\;(I-P_{B})(M+bA+Ba)P_{A}
=[PB​M−PB​M]+[(I−PB)​M​PA−(I−PB)​M​PA]= 0,\displaystyle=\big[P_{B}M-P_{B}M\big]\;+\;\big[(I-P_{B})MP_{A}-(I-P_{B})MP_{A}\big]\;=\;0,

where we substituted the choice of Part 1,

b​A=−(I−PB)​M​[A†​A]=−(I−PB)​M​PA,B​a=−[B​B†]​M=−PB​M,bA=-(I-P_{B})M\,\big[A^{\dagger}A\big]=-(I-P_{B})MP_{A},\qquad Ba=-\big[BB^{\dagger}\big]\,M=-P_{B}M,

and used PB​(I−PB)=0P_{B}(I-P_{B})=0, (I−PB)2=I−PB(I-P_{B})^{2}=I-P_{B}, PA2=PAP_{A}^{2}=P_{A}, etc.. Since ‖δ​B‖F,‖δ​A‖F=O⁡(η)\|\delta B\|_{F},\|\delta A\|_{F}=O(\eta), this pair lies in the domain and attains equality, so it minimizes the leading coefficient, and hence ‖δ​Δ​W⋆−δ​Δ​W‖F\|\delta\Delta W^{\star}-\delta\Delta W\|_{F} to first order.

For Part 2, equality holds only when the three blocks vanish. Since the fourth block of b​A+B​abA+Ba is identically zero by (I−PB)​B=0(I-P_{B})B=0 and A⁡(I−PA)=0A(I-P_{A})=0, the three conditions force

b​A+B​a=−PB​M−(I−PB)​M​PAfor every minimizing pair.bA+Ba\;=\;-\,P_{B}M-(I-P_{B})MP_{A}\qquad\text{for every minimizing pair.}

Consequently, every first-order minimizer satisfies

δ​Δ​W=η⁡(b​A+B​a)+δ​B​δ​A=−η⁡[PB​M+(I−PB)​M​PA]+O⁡(η2),\delta\Delta W\;=\;\eta\,(bA+Ba)+\delta B\,\delta A\;=\;-\eta\big[P_{B}M+(I-P_{B})MP_{A}\big]+O(\eta^{2}),

which is Eq. (38). Finally, if S=O⁡(η)S=O(\eta), the pair (δ​B−B​S,δ​A+S​A)(\delta B-BS,\ \delta A+SA) remains O⁡(η)O(\eta) and satisfies

(δ​B−B​S)​A+B⁡(δ​A+S​A)=δ​B​A+B​δ​A,(\delta B-BS)\,A+B\,(\delta A+SA)=\delta B\,A+B\,\delta A,

so it has the same leading coefficient and is again a first-order minimizer. ∎

Appendix E Learning rate curves

We show learning rate curves for the commonsense runs in Figures 2 (overall commonsense accuracy) and 3 (val. loss). We swept different learning rates for different optimizers, since we found that the optimal learning rate varies between optimizers. The accuracy figures shown in the main text are chosen by taking the optimal learning rate according to loss on a held-out validation set.
